subsystems.name: Scalp sensor array
subsystems.role: picks up the faint electrical and optical signals that leak through the skull.

subsystems.name: Analog front end
subsystems.role: amplifies microvolt signals without drowning them in noise.

subsystems.name: Optical channel (fNIRS)
subsystems.role: measures blood-oxygen changes in the outer cortex as a slower, complementary signal.

subsystems.name: Decoding pipeline
subsystems.role: turns noisy multi-channel signals into a command.

subsystems.name: Feedback and output
subsystems.role: closes the loop so the user can learn to control the system.

subsystems.name: Compute unit
subsystems.role: runs the model, ideally on the headset rather than in the cloud.

buildSteps.title: Choose the signal
buildSteps.detail: Decide whether to read electrical activity with EEG, blood-oxygen with fNIRS, or both; each trades speed against robustness.

buildSteps.title: Make the sensors
buildSteps.detail: Electrodes are printed or moulded from conductive polymer or metal; optical emitters and detectors are packaged at wavelengths that pass through skin and skull.

buildSteps.title: Lay out the headset
buildSteps.detail: Sensors are positioned over the motor and frontal cortex, with enough channels to separate signals but few enough to stay wearable.

buildSteps.title: Build the electronics
buildSteps.detail: Amplifiers, filters, digitisers and shielding are designed to reject mains hum and muscle movement.

buildSteps.title: Collect labelled data
buildSteps.detail: A user performs imagined or real tasks while the system records the resulting patterns, repeated over many sessions.

buildSteps.title: Train and calibrate the decoder
buildSteps.detail: A model is fitted to that person's data, then adapted on the fly as signals drift with fatigue and electrode contact.

buildSteps.title: Close the loop
buildSteps.detail: The decoded command drives a cursor, speller or device, and the visible result lets the user improve control.

buildSteps.title: Validate outside the lab
buildSteps.detail: The headset must work with hair, sweat and movement, over months, before it is anything more than a demonstration.

prerequisites.why: gel electrodes give clean signals but are impractical for daily wear; dry arrays are still noisier.
compact fNIRS units exist, though they only see the outer few millimetres of cortex and respond slowly.
decoders need many hours of recordings from many people; such datasets are scarce.
a headset must classify signals locally, within tens of milliseconds, without a laptop.
it needs gene therapy plus implanted light guides, so it is invasive and not part of any wearable; it is not a route to a non-invasive headset.

pathway.milestone: research and clinical spellers using EEG and fNIRS to pick letters or move a cursor
pathway.unlocks: proof that intent can be read non-invasively, at a few bits per minute.

pathway.milestone: consumer headsets with a small, reliable command set such as selection or attention control
pathway.unlocks: everyday hands-free input for games and accessibility.

pathway.milestone: clinical communication aids for people with paralysis, benchmarked against implanted arrays
pathway.unlocks: a non-surgical alternative for restoring speech or typing.

pathway.milestone: higher-bandwidth non-invasive decoding through better sensors and models, not through optogenetics
pathway.unlocks: general-purpose mental input — if the skull's blurring of signals can be overcome.
